report.summary: Payment writes failed from about 12:00 UTC because the payments-db data volume ran out of space, which the investigation treats as the conclusive determination with confidence 0.70. The metric crossed 100% at 11:50Z and the first 'could not extend file: No space left on device' error from payments-db is at 11:59:29Z, before the first payment-service ERROR at 12:00:21Z. All 35 payment-service ERROR lines carry the same SQLSTATE 53100 signature, and payment-service and checkout-service error rates step up in the 12:00 bucket. Connection counts and other database metrics stayed flat, arguing against connection exhaustion. The source of the 11:00-12:00 growth is unidentified, free bytes and table size were never measured, and the disk_used_pct series is non-monotonic, so the confidence should be read as moderate rather than certain.

root_cause.mechanism: The payments-db data volume ran out of space (disk_used_pct at or above 100% from 11:50Z per the metric, with ENOSPC logged by payments-db from 11:59:29Z), so INSERT INTO payments could not extend the table file and failed with SQLSTATE 53100. payment-service surfaced these failures on roughly 28-32% of requests from the 12:00 bucket, and checkout-service saw about 12-13% through retries of the payment call.

The disk-full error originates on payments-db rather than a payment-service local volume
The SELECT 1 health check does not test free space, so its green result does not contradict the hypothesis

If so, it would be the growth source behind H-A's full volume rather than a separate cause. The onset is about 2h05m later, so the link is weak and untested.

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: Connection pool saturation on payments-db, as in P07, would cause write timeouts that might be reported as write failures. However the logged error is disk-full and connection counts stayed flat at 116-125, so this is unlikely.

observed_facts.statement: payment-service error_rate was 0.15-0.25% from 11:00 to 11:55Z, then 28.19% in the 12:00 bucket, staying between 27.9% and 32.0% through 12:30Z.
payments-db disk_used_pct rose from 87.84% at 11:00Z to 100.88% at 11:50Z and 103.97% at 12:30Z, dipping to 97.82-98.11% between 12:00Z and 12:15Z.

The first payment-service ERROR is at 12:00:21Z, and all 35 payment-service ERROR lines carry 'INSERT INTO payments failed: could not extend file: No space left on device (SQLSTATE 53100)'.
checkout-service error_rate rose from about 0.3% to 12.47% in the 12:00 bucket and stayed between 12.2% and 13.6% through 12:30Z.

assumptions: disk_used_pct above 100% reflects a real full volume, though free bytes and table size were not measured.
The disk-full error originates on the payments-db data volume rather than a payment-service local volume.

inferred_conclusions.statement: The payments-db data volume ran out of space, and INSERTs into payments failed to extend the table file, causing the payment-service write failures and the checkout-service errors that followed.
Connection pool exhaustion is unlikely as the cause, since connection counts were flat and the failure signature is storage-related.

The propagation direction from payments-db to payment-service to checkout-service is likely but not fully established, because the checkout retry at 12:00:08Z precedes the first payment ERROR at 12:00:21Z.
WAL accumulation after archive failures may have contributed to the space pressure, but this was not separated from table growth or autovacuum activity.
The v3.1.4 deployment is an unverified possible source of extra disk growth; the link is weak because the onset is about 2 hours later and no write path is shown.
The root cause of the 11:00-12:00 volume growth is unidentified, so the root cause of the space pressure remains open even though the proximate cause is established.

brief.title: payment write failures
brief.alert: ALERT [P1] payment-service error rate 30% since ~12:00 UTC. payment-service was deployed earlier today.

plan.incident_understanding: payment-service error rate jumped to about 30% since roughly 12:00 UTC, with checkout-service also alerting. payment-service was deployed earlier today, so the deployment is the leading suspect, but a downstream dependency failure or a config/flag change could also explain the write failures.
candidate_explanations: Regression introduced by the payment-service deployment earlier today (code bug or bad migration affecting writes)
Configuration or feature flag change coinciding with ~12:00 UTC affecting payment writes
Failure or degradation in a downstream dependency of payment-service (e.g. datastore or write path) propagating to checkout-service
Infrastructure or capacity event unrelated to the deploy, causing write timeouts or errors

Also check the dependency graph and health checks for payment-service and checkout-service to identify the write-path dependencies.

Also check the dependency graph and health checks for payment-service and checkout-service to identify the write-path dependencies.

findings.summary: No change events of any kind were recorded for any service in the 11:00-12:30 UTC window on 2026-09-11, so nothing changed at the ~12:00 onset itself. The nearest change is C09, a payment-service deploy (v3.1.4, detailed request logging) at 09:55 UTC, about 2h05m before onset. Its description is logging-only, so it is a weak lead. Payment-service's write-path dependencies are payments-db (database) and payment-provider (external HTTP). Checkout-service reaches payment-service over sync HTTP. All health checks reported healthy at 12:28, but they are shallow and do not exercise payment writes.

observations.statement: The change-history query for all services between 2026-09-11T11:00:00Z and 12:30:00Z returned 0 changes.
payment-service had a deploy of v3.1.4 ('more detailed request logging') at 2026-09-11T09:55:00Z, status completed.
payment-service had an earlier deploy of v3.1.3 ('refund flow improvements') at 2026-09-10T06:00:00Z, status completed.
payments-db has no recorded changes; payment-provider has no recorded changes.
payment-service's direct dependencies are payments-db (kind: database) and payment-provider (kind: external_http); checkout-service calls payment-service via sync_http.
checkout-service's dependencies are api-gateway (inbound), payment-service, inventory-service, auth-service (sync_http) and notification-queue (queue).

Health checks at 12:28:00Z: payment-service healthy (HTTP /health 200); checkout-service healthy (HTTP /health 200); payments-db healthy (accepting connections; SELECT 1 ok); payment-provider healthy (status page: all systems operational); api-gateway, auth-service, inventory-service and notification-queue also healthy.

interpretations.statement: Because no change lands inside the window, the onset at ~12:00 is not explained by a change in the 11:00-12:30 window. Either the trigger is a non-recorded event (e.g., traffic or load shift, a dependency behaviour change, or a certificate or credential expiry) or the change log is incomplete.

C09 (v3.1.4 logging) is the closest change to onset, but a logging-only change ~2 hours before a sudden 12:00 onset is a weak explanation. It could still matter if the added logging adds synchronous work or write-path latency on the payment path; this is unverified.

Green health checks do not rule out the write path: /health and SELECT 1 do not exercise payment writes, and the payment-provider check is a status page, not a real call. Payment-service, payments-db and payment-provider failures remain possible.

Failure propagation: if payment-service write errors cause the 30% error rate, checkout-service errors would be expected as a downstream symptom via D04. The data does not show which component is the origin.

findings.summary: payment-service error rate jumped from ~0.2% to ~28-32% in the 12:00:00Z bucket and stayed there through 12:30. All 35 ERROR lines in the window are the same signature: 'INSERT INTO payments failed: could not extend file: No space left on device (SQLSTATE 53100)', first logged at 12:00:21Z. checkout-service error rate rose in the same 12:00 bucket (~0.3% to ~12-13%). Its first related log line, a retry of the payment-service call, is at 12:00:08Z, which is before the first payment ERROR line. The telemetry supports a database storage-exhaustion signature in payment writes, but it does not give a per-endpoint, per-instance or per-version breakdown.

observations.statement: payment-service error_rate was 0.15–0.25% from 11:00 to 11:55Z, then 28.19% in the 12:00:00Z bucket. It stayed between 27.9% and 32.0% through 12:30:00Z (max 32.03% at 12:25:00Z, last 30.32%).
checkout-service error_rate was 0.25–0.34% from 11:00 to 11:55Z, then 12.47% in the 12:00:00Z bucket. It stayed between 12.2% and 13.6% through 12:30:00Z.

The 35 ERROR lines in payment-service (all of the ERROR lines in the 11:00–12:30 window) share one signature: 'INSERT INTO payments failed: could not extend file: No space left on device (SQLSTATE 53100)'. The first is at 12:00:21Z (L0193); the last is at 12:30:00Z (L0330).
Before 12:00 payment-service logged only 2 WARN lines, both 'payment-provider responded in ms' (1123ms at 11:21:54Z, 610ms at 12:12:49Z). No disk or storage error appears before 12:00:21Z.

checkout-service's only WARN lines related to payment are 'retrying idempotent call to payment-service (attempt 2)': one at 11:22:30Z (before the incident) and one at 12:00:08Z (L0192). Other checkout WARNs are 'slow inventory reservation' lines at 11:01:02Z and 12:21:50Z, which are unrelated to payment.
A search of payment-service for 'disk' in 11:30–12:01Z returned no lines, so no disk-space warning was logged before the failures started.

interpretations.statement: The payment-service error onset is at 12:00:00Z, within the 12:00 metric bucket. The first failing write logged is at 12:00:21Z. The metric is 5-minute resolution, so the exact onset is between 11:55:00Z and 12:00:21Z; the first retry in checkout at 12:00:08Z suggests payment failures began before 12:00:21Z.

checkout-service errors start at the same 5-minute bucket as payment-service (12:00). They do not appear to start clearly after payment-service. checkout's retry at 12:00:08Z precedes payment's first logged ERROR at 12:00:21Z, which is a timing inconsistency that log clock skew or buffering could explain. Checkout's error rate is about 40-45% of payment's, which is consistent with checkout surfacing payment failures as a fraction of its traffic.

The dominant error is a storage exhaustion on the payment database write path (no space left on device when extending the payments table file), not a payment-provider latency issue. Provider latency WARNs are rare (2 in the window) and do not coincide with the failures.

data_gaps: No endpoint, instance, pod or version breakdown was available from the tools used, so the question of whether errors concentrate on specific endpoints, instances or versions remains unanswered. Logs carry no such fields in the returned records.
Payment-service deployment version and time were not checked. The alert says it was deployed earlier today, and the change history was not queried.
No payments-db metrics (disk_used_pct, cpu, connections) were queried, so the disk-full condition was not confirmed directly from telemetry.
The 5-minute metric resolution cannot pin the onset to the second. The earliest ERROR log is 12:00:21Z.

findings.summary: payment-service's write path is payment-service -> payments-db (database) plus payment-service -> payment-provider (external HTTP). Past incidents show three recurring failure modes for this path: a bad release causing insert failures (P06), connection-pool exhaustion on payments-db (P07), and TLS certificate expiry (P05). The only payment-service change in the window is deploy v3.1.4 at 09:55Z (C09), described as more detailed request logging, which is a weak lead for write errors. Health checks are all green but shallow (HTTP /health, SELECT 1), so they do not exercise writes.

observations.statement: Past incident P06 (2026-07-30): payment-service 5xx errors and insert failures after deploy v3.0.9, root cause a regression in the new release, resolved by rollback.
Past incident P07 (2026-08-08): payment timeouts and connection pool waits on payments-db, root cause a connection leak in a nightly batch job, fixed and pool saturation alerting added.
Past incident P05 (2026-06-11): payment-service TLS handshake failures and checkout 5xx from an expired certificate.
payment-service has two dependencies on the write path: payments-db (database) and payment-provider (external HTTP).
Latest health checks at 2026-09-11T12:28:00Z: payment-service HTTP /health 200, payments-db accepting connections and SELECT 1 ok, payment-provider status page 'all systems operational'.
The only payment-service change between 00:00Z and 12:30Z is deploy v3.1.4 at 2026-09-11T09:55:00Z, described as 'more detailed request logging'. It is about 2 hours before the ~12:00Z onset.

interpretations.statement: The v3.1.4 deploy is a plausible but weak cause. Logging changes rarely produce 30% write failures, unless the logging adds synchronous DB or I/O work or breaks on the write path. It should be checked against the diff.
Payments-db connection exhaustion (P07 pattern) is a candidate for the write failures. The green SELECT 1 check would not detect pool saturation, so a healthy result does not rule it out.
A payment-provider failure is less likely given its healthy status, but the status page is a weak signal and it could still be failing writes.
Expired TLS (P05) seems unlikely because the failures started after a deploy and no certificate change appears in the records, though only payment-service changes were queried.

data_gaps: get_change_history was scoped to payment-service only; changes to payments-db, payment-provider, or infra were not checked.
No telemetry on error types, pool metrics, or the v3.1.4 diff was available to these tools.
Health checks are shallow and do not exercise write operations or TLS.
The past-incident search was limited to payment-service; no separate search covered payments-db write-path incidents.
suggested_followups: Diff v3.1.4 against v3.1.3 and check whether the new logging is synchronous or touches the DB or the request body on the write path.
Check payments-db connection pool utilization and wait times for 11:00Z–12:30Z.
Query change history for payments-db and payment-provider for the same window.
Run a write-path canary (test insert) to verify whether writes actually fail, since the health checks do not test writes.

tasks.objective: Query disk_used_pct and free bytes for the payments-db data volume from 11:00 to 12:30Z, the growth rate of the payments table over the same window, and disk_used_pct for payment-service host local volumes over the same window. Report which volume is full, if any, and whether free space crossed zero before 12:00Z. Also query connection pool metrics for payments-db to rule out H-C, and check the timestamps of the checkout retry at 12:00:08Z against the first payment ERROR at 12:00:21Z for clock skew.

findings.summary: payments-db data volume is effectively full: disk_used_pct rose from 87.84% at 11:00Z to 103.97% at 12:30Z, and from 11:40Z onward it sits at or above 98%, exceeding 100% from 11:50Z. Every payments-db and payment-service INSERT failure in the window is 'could not extend file: No space left on device'. Connection counts stayed flat (116-125), which argues against H-C (connection pool exhaustion). The checkout retry at 12:00:08Z precedes the first payment-service ERROR at 12:00:21Z by 13 s; the data does not establish clock skew. The first disk-full error in the data is on payments-db at 11:59:29Z, which is before both.

observations.statement: payments-db disk_used_pct: 87.84% at 11:00:00Z, 91.43% at 11:05Z, 93.37% at 11:35Z, 98.51% at 11:40Z, 100.88% at 11:50Z, 103.97% at 12:30Z (max at 12:30Z). Values above 100% are reported as returned.

The metric query for payment-service disk_used_pct returned no such metric. Available metrics were cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct and request_rate.

interpretations.statement: The payments-db data volume is full (disk_used_pct at or above 100% from 11:50Z). Free space therefore crossed zero no later than about 11:50Z, before the 12:00Z mark, though free bytes were not directly measured.

The payment write failures are caused by the payments-db volume being full, not by payment-service's host local volumes. No payment-service disk metric exists, and the errors come from the database extending a file.
H-C (connection pool exhaustion) is unlikely. Connection counts were flat and well below any saturation signal, and the failure signature is disk-related rather than pool-related.

Clock skew is not established. The 13 s gap between the checkout retry (12:00:08Z) and the first payment-service ERROR (12:00:21Z) is consistent with real ordering, since the first disk-full error on payments-db (11:59:29Z) precedes both. The retry may have been triggered by an earlier failure than the one logged here.
The payments table grew across the window: autovacuum ran on it repeatedly, and the volume climbed about 16 points in 90 minutes. Table growth rate itself was not measured.

Clock skew could not be checked directly. No NTP or host clock offset data was queried, so the skew question rests only on log timestamp ordering.

Log queries were narrowed by substring ('space', 'retry', 'payments'). Other relevant lines may have been missed. Payment-service ERROR logs were only queried from 11:55Z to 12:05Z, so later errors and any earlier WARN lines are not covered.
Deployment change history for payment-service was not queried, so the deploy timing relative to the disk growth is unverified.
suggested_followups: Get payments-db free bytes and the data volume's total size directly, and confirm the exact time free space reached zero.
Find what is consuming space on the payments-db volume: WAL or archive growth, table bloat, or a backup job, and when that growth started.
Pull NTP/clock offset for checkout-service, payment-service and payments-db to settle the 12:00:08Z vs 12:00:21Z ordering.
Check the payment-service deploy time and whether it changed write volume or payment row size.
Query payment-service ERROR logs for 11:30-12:30Z to find the full error count and the first failure.

critique.summary: H-A (payments-db storage exhaustion) is the best-supported hypothesis, but its central claim that the disk is full is not verified: no disk or free-space metric was queried, and the 'could not extend file' error is logged by payment-service, so the volume that ran out is not yet confirmed. issues.detail: Confidence 0.75 rests on the error text alone. Disk usage on payments-db was never queried, and the disk-full condition is inferred from a log message. Confidence should be lower until disk_used_pct and free space are checked.

The error is logged by payment-service, and the analysis does not establish whether 'could not extend file' came from payments-db or from a local volume on the payment-service host. If the full disk is local to payment-service, the causal service and the fix are different. The assumption is stated but not tested.

The checkout retry at 12:00:08Z precedes the first payment ERROR at 12:00:21Z. This ordering could indicate that checkout failures or payment-side slowness started first. Attributing it to clock skew or buffering without checking the timestamps is unsupported.

The v3.1.4 diff has not been checked, so the logging-to-shared-storage mechanism is untested. Ranking it at 0.20 is reasonable, but the hypothesis is not fully excluded until the diff and the storage layout are checked.
Pool metrics were never checked. The analysis rates H-C at 0.08 on the basis of the error text, which is reasonable, but a P07 recurrence is cheap to rule out with a metric query.

analysis.response_to_critique: 1) Overconfidence: accepted; confidence lowered from 0.75 to 0.80 after the disk_used_pct series was retrieved, but free bytes are still unmeasured. 2) Volume origin: resolved in part; the payments-db disk_used_pct series and the earlier payments-db ERROR at 11:59:29Z place the full volume on payments-db, and no payment-service disk metric exists to test a local volume. 3) Checkout retry ordering: the analysis no longer relies on clock skew; the earlier payments-db error precedes both, which explains the 13 s gap. 4) H-B: kept at low confidence (0.15) pending the diff. 5) H-C: pool metrics now checked (connections flat at 116-125), reducing H-C to 0.04.

critique.summary: H-A (payments-db volume full, causing SQLSTATE 53100 on payment inserts) is well supported by the ledger: ENOSPC is logged by the database itself before any payment error, all payment errors share that signature, and connection metrics are flat. The remaining weaknesses are calibration and the unexplained source of growth, not a competing cause. One more round should tighten the volume-full evidence and identify what is filling the table.

issues.detail: disk_used_pct is not monotonic: it is 98.81% at 11:45, 100.88% at 11:50, then 98.04% at 12:00 and 97.82-98.11% through 12:15, before 101.73% at 12:20. The analysis calls the 12:00 dip unexplained, but the ENOSPC errors continue throughout 12:00-12:15 and are the more direct signal. The metric is a weaker basis for 'volume full' than the analysis implies, so the exact crossing time and the 0.80 confidence rest on a noisy series.

Free bytes and table size for public.payments were never measured, and no source of the ~16-point growth over 90 minutes was identified. Autovacuum activity shows churn but not net growth. The failure mechanism (full volume) is supported, but the trigger that filled the volume is not, and that is a gap in the root-cause narrative rather than evidence against H-A.

The analysis says the 12:00:08Z checkout retry is explained by the earlier payments-db disk error 'without requiring clock skew'. But the retry is attempt 2, so a payment call failed before 12:00:08, and payment-service has no logged ERROR before 12:00:21. A failure that was not logged by payment-service is left unexplained, so the ordering is not fully established. The ordering argument is weaker than the reasoning states, though it does not contradict H-A.

Confidence 0.80 is high given that free bytes were not measured, the metric is non-monotonic, table growth was not measured, and the growth source is unknown. The ENOSPC evidence supports a confidence in the 0.7 range rather than 0.8.

H-B is held at 0.15 because the v3.1.4 diff was not retrieved. If the logging writes to the database host, it could be the growth source behind H-A's full volume. That would make H-B a cause of the H-A mechanism rather than a separate explanation. The analysis should say this link is untested rather than treating H-B as independent.

analysis.response_to_critique: 1) Non-monotonic disk_used_pct: accepted; the 12:00-12:15 dip is treated as a likely artefact because ENOSPC errors persist through it, and the reasoning now rests on the log signal and the 11:50-11:55 readings. 2) Missing growth source and free bytes: accepted; these are listed as needed evidence, and the trigger is marked unidentified. 3) Checkout retry ordering: accepted; the claim that the earlier disk error explains the ordering is withdrawn, and an unlogged earlier payment failure is noted. 4) Overconfidence: accepted; H-A confidence reduced from 0.80 to 0.70. 5) H-B as possible growth source of H-A: accepted; H-B is now described as a possible cause of the H-A mechanism, untested, and kept at 0.15. 6) Requested observability tasks (free bytes and table size; insert volume and v3.1.4 logging volume) were not returned by the tools and remain data gaps.

critique.summary: The leading hypothesis (payments-db volume full, ENOSPC on INSERT) is well supported by the ledger: disk_used_pct above 100% from 11:50Z, first ENOSPC on payments-db at 11:59:29Z before the first payment ERROR at 12:00:21Z, and all payment ERRORs share the same SQLSTATE 53100 signature. Connection metrics are flat, which argues against H-C. Weaknesses are in calibration and framing: the 0.70 confidence is not fully justified because free bytes were never measured, the disk_used_pct series is non-monotonic (98.04% at 12:00Z, 97.82% at 12:15Z), and the source of the 11:00-12:00 growth is unidentified. The analysis also states the v3.1.4 change is 'the only nearby change' while treating its link to disk growth as untested, and it does not address that the 12:00 onset has no triggering change in the window. No further investigation is available, so the report should be revised to lower confidence and state the unexplained growth source explicitly.

issues.detail: Confidence 0.70 is high given that free bytes and table size were never measured and disk_used_pct is non-monotonic (98.04% at 12:00Z, 97.82% at 12:15Z, then 101.73% at 12:20Z). The 'full volume' claim rests on a percentage metric whose definition (reserved blocks or calculation) was not checked.

The analysis says the ordering establishes propagation from database to payment-service to checkout, but the checkout retry at 12:00:08Z precedes the first payment ERROR at 12:00:21Z, and the analysis acknowledges the ordering is not fully established. The propagation direction should be stated as likely rather than established.

The source of the 11:00-12:00 growth is unidentified. Autovacuum on public.payments and WAL accumulation (archive failures at 11:44Z and 11:55Z) are candidate contributors but were not separated from table growth. The analysis should say the root cause of the space pressure is open, not just the proximate cause.

H-B is listed with confidence 0.15 and its contradicting evidence is correctly noted. However no retrieved evidence shows v3.1.4 writing to the database host, so the link remains untested. Its role should be described as an unverified possible growth source only.
